title: Strings and the operations that quietly cost O(n)

claims.text: The encoding now standard was designed by Ken Thompson of the Plan 9 group at Bell Labs and outlined on 2 September 1992; Pike and Thompson implemented it within days and converted the system to use it throughout. It was first presented publicly at the USENIX conference in January 1993.

source.title: Pike, R. and Thompson, K., Hello World or Καλημέρα κόσμε, Proceedings of the Winter 1993 USENIX Conference

claims.text: The problem the design addressed is stated in the paper: without reading from the start of a string it was impossible to find character boundaries. Thompson’s modification made the encoding self-synchronising, so a reader can start anywhere and immediately detect character boundaries, at the cost of being somewhat less bit-efficient than the proposal it replaced.

source.title: Pike, R. and Thompson, K., Hello World or Καλημέρα κόσμε, Proceedings of the Winter 1993 USENIX Conference

claims.text: The encoding is variable length, and the earlier scheme it replaced lacked both self-synchronisation and fully compatible handling of characters such as the slash; seven-bit characters represent only themselves, with multi-byte sequences using only bytes that have the high bit set.

source.title: Pike, R. and Thompson, K., Hello World or Καλημέρα κόσμε, Proceedings of the Winter 1993 USENIX Conference

beats.broke: a string looks like an array of characters and is not one, so operations that appear to be indexing are searches
beats.fix: know which unit your language indexes by — byte, code unit, or character — and know that they coincide only for text that happens to be simple
beats.cost: the cheap-looking operations are linear, and building a string by repeated concatenation turns a loop into a quadratic one
beats.interview: why taking the length of a string is not always a constant-time operation
